rows.episode_title: A Whole Bot of Fun / Volunteer Bot
rows.synopsis: Doug and Emma search all over Mega City to find a lost tennis ball.
rows.situation: Doug, a boy robot who has never heard of fun, delivers a table tennis ball to Emma and asks the question his processors were never set for: why do people play games? Then the demonstration ball escapes into an adults-only office tower and a ball pit, and the promised lesson looks lost.
rows.coping: Emma refuses to let the ball define the day: two kids become one grown-up by the power of math (deep voice, 'morning, coffee, mortgages'), they swim a ball pit hunting it, and when the ball bounces away for good she discovers the real answer out loud: the fun was already happening. Skating, disguises, pit-diving. Doug learns the word, the game, and the hug that says 'we care.'
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: disguise and ball-pit slapstick plays 2-4; the chase-the-thing-and-miss-the-fun insight and the hug lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'search for a lost tennis ball' is the plot skeleton; the script is a first-fun arc with a fake-mustache-free grown-up disguise, the chasing-fun-while-having-it turn, and a first hug.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Doug is a boy robot with a delivery to make and a big question: why do humans play games? Emma has the answer in one word, fun, and a demonstration that goes sideways fast when their table tennis ball ricochets into an office tower full of grown-ups. Two kids, one deep-voiced disguise, and a swim through a ball pit later, the ball is gone, and Emma realizes something better: they never needed it. The fun had been happening the whole time, and Doug heads home knowing a new word, a new friend, and a new way to say you care.

rows.episode_title: A Whole Bot of Fun / Volunteer Bot
rows.synopsis: As the city library prepares to open, Doug and Emma think of ways to help.
rows.situation: Doug and Emma sign up to volunteer at the dilapidated library and then can't find a single job that's actually theirs: grape jelly painted on a wall (it looked like purple paint) defeats their scrubbing, Mop Bot cleans it better, and Dad sorts the books better too. The celebration starts and they haven't helped at all.
rows.coping: Every failure was actually the method: each time they couldn't do the job, they asked the exact right helper, from Mop Bot to Dad. At the ceremony the organizers name them the special volunteers and say why: asking for help brought everyone together. Doug immediately tries his new skill on Dad's mountain of unsorted reboots.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: jelly-mess comedy plays 2-4; the asking-is-helping lesson and the letdown-before-the-credit beat land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'think of ways to help' hides the shape of it, three failed direct attempts that were secretly successes, and the public credit turn that names the lesson.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The city library needs volunteers, and Doug and Emma arrive bursting with incredible-ness. But the jelly-wall is too sticky for their scrubbing, the book-sorting has too many books, and a very happy Mop Bot takes the mop. By the time the grand opening starts, the two are certain they did nothing at all. Then the speeches begin, and the secret of volunteering comes out: every expert who fixed the library came because Doug and Emma asked. Asking for help is helping, and Doug has one more delivery to make, straight to his dad's sorting pile.

rows.episode_title: Bot on the Beach / Bot of the Party
rows.synopsis: Emma takes Doug on a beach day to show him why people love it.
rows.situation: Emma answers Doug's beach question with a bag of gear and a checklist: do every beach activity there is before sunset. Snacks, paddleboarding, merbot leg-burying, sandcastles, and then a very, very big wave soaks the whole bag, and the clock beats them both.
rows.coping: Staring at people doing nothing at all cracks it open: relaxing is the beach activity nobody packed. Sprawled on warm sand listening to waves, Doug calls it his favorite thing yet, then brings the discovery home as Rebots Beach for his worn-out parents.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: beach-activity romp plays 2-4; the checklist-versus-stillness insight lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'show him why people love it' omits the do-it-all checklist structure, the gear-destroying wave, and that the answer is the one activity Emma forgot to plan.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Doug has never met a beach, so Emma packs a bag big enough to prove the point: snacks, paddleboards, sandcastles, the works, every activity before sunset. The checklist zips along nicely until a monster wave soaks the gear and the sun starts dropping on their ambitions. Then Doug notices the strangest beach-goers of all, the ones doing nothing, and learns the one beach activity you don't need equipment for. The day ends at Rebots Beach, where two very busy robot parents learn to unwind, gears going loose.

rows.episode_title: Bot on the Beach / Bot of the Party
rows.synopsis: Doug and Emma try to track down missing supplies for a big party.
rows.situation: Jenny Droneberg is about to make her 1,000th delivery, and Emma throws her a real party: limbo, snack table, musical chairs. Then Safety Bot, doing his job with maximum dedication, reboots every unsafe item into hard hats and dull snacks, and the party looks wrecked.
rows.coping: The mystery of the missing supplies ends with a confession rather than a culprit hunt, and Jenny settles it herself: her favorite part was always the people, not the piñata. The bots turn Safety Bot's reboot booth into a photo booth, so the bot who almost ruined the party gets included in the picture.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: party-game romp plays 2-4; the accidentally-ruined-by-good-intentions turn and the include-the-left-out-bot coda land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'track down missing supplies' is the mid-episode mystery; the script's spine is Safety Bot's reboot spree, Jenny's friends-are-the-party verdict, and the photo-booth repair.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Jenny Droneberg has made 999 deliveries, and the bots plan to celebrate with a handshake and an early bedtime. Emma has better ideas: limbo, snacks, musical chairs. Everything goes perfectly until Safety Bot, true to his name, reboots the dangerously fun party into safety hats and caution tape. But Jenny never misses the piñata at all: her thousandth delivery was best celebrated with friends, and the party that survives is part photo shoot, part apology, with Safety Bot right in the frame.

rows.episode_title: Vacation Bots / Bots of the Forest
rows.synopsis: When Emma's family vacation is canceled, she and Doug make a new plan.
rows.situation: The seaside vacation is fully planned, pool, mini golf, the Super Duper Zuper coaster, the picnic under the stars, and then rain cancels every flight, with Mom rained in on the far side of it. Dad goes quiet doing dishes, and the family's favorite part is the one that got away.
rows.coping: They rebuild the whole vacation at home: hotel pool becomes bathtub pool, mini golf and the coaster become household constructions, and the missed picnic under the stars gets saved by the twinkly lights Doug packed without knowing why. The verdict renames the day: a staycation, because vacations are about having a great time together, not going places.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: home-recreation comedy plays 2-4; the noticed-sadness beat (Dad quiet at the sink) and the together-not-places lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make a new plan' is the shape; the script supplies the specific recreations, the forgotten-favorite wrinkle, and the packed-lights payoff.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Emma has the family vacation memorized down to the roller coaster, and the rain cancels all of it: no flights, no hotel pool, no beach picnic, and a mom stuck on the wrong side of the storm. But a Pine family vacation has survived worse. The bathtub becomes the hotel pool, suitcases become the Super Robo Zuper, and when Doug spots Dad's quiet disappointment, the missing piece turns out to be the one Doug accidentally packed: a picnic under twinkly-light stars, and a new word for a vacation that never left the house.

rows.episode_title: Vacation Bots / Bots of the Forest
rows.synopsis: Doug and his dad get lost on a hike and try to find their way home.
rows.situation: Doug and Bob Bot hike into the woods trusting their robo maps, until a very large moose chases them deep enough that the maps go dead. Officially lost, Dad declares them bots of the forest and starts building a house, and the way home is anything but clear.
rows.coping: Lost and mapless, they still work the problem: retracing steps, then a rescue by hikers Kath and Barb, who teach the whole toolkit, trail blazes, a compass (never eat soggy waffles), the setting sun, and the North Star. Back home, Doug installs a blaze system through the Rebots warehouse so nobody has to be lost to learn it.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: moose-chase and fort-building comedy plays 2-4; the layered wayfinding teaching (blazes, compass, sun, stars) lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'get lost and try to find their way home' is accurate; the script adds Dad's stay-and-settle comedy, the named navigation curriculum, and the blaze-installation coda.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A hike with Dad starts with moss, wildflowers, and one enormously alarming moose, and ends with two robots genuinely, officially lost, their robo maps dead in the deep woods. Dad copes by declaring a new life in the wilderness, complete with a leaf-TV house, until real hikers Kath and Barb arrive and turn the rescue into a masterclass: trail blazes, a compass, the setting sun, and finally the North Star. Safely home, Doug wires the lesson into the warehouse walls, because every maze, he says, can use a blaze.

rows.episode_title: A Bot's Best Friend / A Bot in His Natural Habitat
rows.synopsis: Doug takes care of Emma's dog to find out why people like pets.
rows.situation: Doug delivers a pet dish and arrives at the Pine house mid-crisis: Mr. Pine's lucky audition shoes are missing, the dog is barking to get inside, and Doug is holding the leash of an animal that runs like a rocket and drags him straight through a mud puddle.
rows.coping: Doug works through the whole job of a pet person, feeding, playing, walking, bathing, and the dog solves the shoe mystery herself: she was trying to get inside because she knew where the lucky shoes were all along. The lesson lands with a question for his parents: can we get a pet? And the family gains a Critter Bot.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: dog-walk slapstick and bath comedy plays 2-4; the care-works-both-ways insight (she was taking care of us) lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'why people like pets' undersells the arc, the shoe mystery resolves through the dog's own knowing, and the episode ends with Doug asking for a pet of his own.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A pet dish delivery turns into Doug's first shift as a dog person. Princess Woofingham needs feeding, playing, walking, and a very splashy bath, and Doug is learning on the job while Mr. Pine tears the house apart looking for the lucky shoes he needs for his big audition. Nobody guesses who actually knows where the shoes are, the dog has been trying to say so all day. By the end, Doug can answer his own big question about why people have pets, and he heads home with a request his parents did not see coming.

rows.episode_title: A Bot's Best Friend / A Bot in His Natural Habitat
rows.segment_title: A Bot in His Natural Habitat
rows.synopsis: Emma and Doug make a new home for a stray duckling.
rows.situation: A baby duckling turns up in Emma's backyard, far from any pond, and the kids name him Quackerino. Craft-supply homes and a kiddie-pool pond both miss the mark, and the littlest critic stays unhappy in each one.
rows.coping: When Doug's antenna picks up distant quacking, the plan changes from building a home to finding one: waddling like a duck, they lead Quackerino to a real pond and his family. The habitat lesson lands at home plate, an animal's natural home has everything it truly needs, and Doug decides his own favorite habitat is home with his parents.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: quacking, crafting, and waddle-comedy plays 2-4; the habitat-versus-made-home distinction and the goodbye-at-the-pond beat land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make a new home for a stray duckling' hides that the made homes fail on purpose, twice, before the family reunion gives the real answer.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Emma's backyard nature shoot finds the most adorable baby duckling either of them has ever seen, and naming him Quackerino is the easy part. The hard part is home: a glitter-dusted craft nest flops, a rebooted kiddie-pool pond with matching lily pads flops harder, and the little duck still is not happy. Then Doug's antenna catches a sound only ducks can answer, and the right move stops being building and starts being leading, waddle by waddle, to a real pond where a whole family is waiting.

rows.episode_title: Shop 'Til Ya Bot / Adventure Bots
rows.synopsis: Emma's dad finds a way to show Emma and Doug how errands can be fun.
rows.situation: Doug and Emma are dragged grocery shopping with a list of must-haves, a deli counter stuck at number 3 while they hold ticket 20, and Mr. Pine promising a mystery surprise. The Swiss cheese wait alone stretches seventeen numbers long, and the race to beat ticket number 20 ends one number short.
rows.coping: The loss flips into the reveal: they were on a scavenger hunt the whole time, and a scavenger hunt is a game where you look for things on a list. The game was the point, not the prize. Doug banks the bigger lesson, anything can be turned into a game, and immediately builds one: an obstacle course that turns Uncle Forkrick's repetitive box-moving job into fun that never shuts down.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: melon-sniffing and basket-shots comedy plays 2-4; the numbers-wait frustration, the one-number miss, and the anything-can-be-a-game reframe land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'errands can be fun' names the moral; the script supplies the deli-ticket race, the scavenger-hunt reveal, the self-checkout surprise, and the Forkrick coda.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Grocery day sounds like the least fun words Doug has ever heard, and Emma agrees until her dad turns the list into a challenge. There are melons to sniff and squeeze, top-shelf baskets to sink from robo-springs, a freezer to brave for froyo, and a deli ticket two numbers from losing it all. When the last item is missed by exactly one ticket number, Mr. Pine lets the secret out: the errand was a scavenger hunt all along, and the surprise at the end is the best one, the self-checkout machine, plus a brand-new game for a very overworked Uncle Forkrick.

rows.episode_title: Shop 'Til Ya Bot / Adventure Bots
rows.synopsis: Emma shows Doug how to use his imagination while looking for a lost item.
rows.situation: Mom's Giz-Go invention escapes and zooms through Rebots, and Doug promised to catch it. Emma reframes the chase as an epic adventure from the Gemstone Joan books, but Doug's imagination is not an app he can download, and the snowcapped mountain she sees is, to his sensors, an ordinary ramp.
rows.coping: Emma teaches the rule that does not need a plug: pretend, don't plug in, and picture something more adventure-y than what you see. The ramp becomes a mountain, the floor becomes lava (safely mopped by Safety Bot), and when the power cuts out, headlamp pretend-work turns a dark warehouse into a tunnel, a runaway mine cart into a catchable target, and a cargo net into the finish of Doug's first real adventure.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lava-hopping and mine-cart chase plays 2-4; the imagination-lesson meta-craft (pretend, not plug in) and the lose-the-chase-win-the-game structure land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'use his imagination while looking for a lost item' is the frame; the script adds the pretend-not-plug-in teaching, the Safety Bot interlude, and the mom's jungle-weeding coda.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Doug promised to catch his mom's runaway Giz-Go, and Emma has decided the chase counts as an adventure, Gemstone Joan hats and all. One problem: Doug cannot see the mountains she sees, because imagination is not an app. Then the lesson takes, a ramp becomes a peak, a floor becomes lava, and a blackout becomes a tunnel chase with a runaway mine cart. By the time the cargo net comes down, Doug has caught the invention, earned the name adventure buddy, and left his mom wondering why weeding the garden suddenly feels like a jungle expedition.

rows.episode_title: Bot on the Farm / Bot-Cycle Built for Two
rows.synopsis: Doug and Emma learn about farming while visiting Doug's grandbots.
rows.situation: Armed with a library book and a full plug-in download, Doug and Emma declare themselves the Farming Dream Team and take over the farm for the day, right up until a robo-vacuum mangles the blueberry patch and the cows simply will not listen, then bolt entirely.
rows.coping: Nana and Grandbot take the runaway-cow disaster gently: you are not supposed to know everything, and some things can only be learned by doing, over time, with experience. They hand over their earned tricks (a special sound, an ear scratch, following the food), and Doug's new digi-book leaves pages deliberately blank, because there is always more to learn.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: blueberry-vacuum and cow-chase slapstick plays 2-4; the knowing-versus-experience lesson and the blank-pages coda land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'learn about farming' hides the know-it-all setup, the two failures, and the grandbots' experience lesson that reframes the whole visit.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Doug and Emma arrive at the grandbots' farm knowing everything there is to know, one from a book, one from a download, and volunteer to run the place for the day. The blueberries fight back, the apples need actual tools, and the cows go rogue at full speed. The rescue comes from the farmers who have been at this for years, and their secret is not a fact at all: some things you can only learn by doing. The pie gets baked, the cows get milked, and Doug's new digi-book goes home with blank pages on purpose.

rows.episode_title: Bot on the Farm / Bot-Cycle Built for Two
rows.synopsis: When Doug sees Emma's bike, he tries learning how to ride.
rows.situation: Emma teaches Doug to ride his new bike in four steps, pedaling, balancing, steering, stopping, and it is going perfectly until Emma takes a fall. The bot who never falls is suddenly the one too scared to get back on, and she hides it so she will not stop Doug from riding.
rows.coping: Critter Bot quietly relays Emma's secret, and Doug does not tease or push: he names it, offers the out, then gives exactly the help she asks for. With a steadying hand and a five-count eject, the lightning is back on the thunder, and the teacher thanks the student for getting her back on her bike.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: bike-training montage plays 2-4; the fear-after-a-fall beat, hiding it to protect someone else, and the role reversal land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'he tries learning how to ride' is half the story; the script's heart is Emma's fall, her hidden fear, and the student-becomes-teacher ending.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Doug has a shiny new bike called the Robo-Racer and a teacher who has never fallen, which makes the lesson look easy until it happens to her instead. One spill and Emma is done, secretly scared, and quietly steering Doug toward riding alone so he will not stop. Critter Bot has other ideas, and soon the student is doing the steadying: a held bike, a countdown, and the wind back in Emma's gears, with both of them agreeing the day needed the other one.

rows.episode_title: Bots for Dinner / It's the Bot That Counts
rows.synopsis: Doug goes out with Emma's family and learns about eating at restaurants.
rows.situation: Two robot families and the Pines meet at a real restaurant for the first time, and the bots bring their own operating manual: dancing to the ambient music, reading the menu as a bedtime story, mistaking silverware for table instruments, then dropping the whole set in a celebratory cheer with dinner still unstarted.
rows.coping: Emma, restaurant expert on six visits' experience, coaches without laughing at the errors, and the crisis of the dropped silverware turns into the discovery: a restaurant is about more than food, it is about getting to know each other while you wait. More silverware is askable. Doug brings the lesson home by turning the recharge room into a charge-and-chat spot for his grandbots' visit.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: robot-at-restaurant mistake comedy plays 2-4; the waiting-well beat and the talking-is-the-point lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'learns about eating at restaurants' undersells the error pile-up, the silverware drop, and the conversation reframing that resolves it. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
rows.per_story_synopsis: The Bot family's first restaurant has music, a giant food book, tiny blankets for your lap, and one very confused robot family, and Emma, with her six visits of expertise, is the only translator. They nail their orders, survive the hardest part (waiting), and then cheer so hard the silverware hits the floor. Which is when the whole evening gets re-read: the meal was never the point, the talking was, and a refill of forks is one polite ask away. Doug likes the idea enough to install a recharge-and-chat room back at Rebots.

rows.episode_title: Bots for Dinner / It's the Bot That Counts
rows.synopsis: Doug's nana has a case of the glitches, so he and Emma make her a card.
rows.situation: Nana's visit is canceled because she is low and needs an upgrade day, and Doug has confetti waiting for a grandbot who is not coming. Project Pick-Me-Up launches: a card rebooted from old newspaper, a secret beep-boop message, a daisy from memory, and a painted starry sky, until a goat with a love of chewing gets the delivery.
rows.coping: The card arrives ruined, and the confession of what it was supposed to be, daisy from the day they met, blue like her favorite color, turns out to be the pick-me-up itself. Nana feels loved and cared for, Doug learns the real pickup was showing the love, and the helpers discover cheering Nana up picked them up too.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: goat-chase comedy plays 2-4; the sick-grandparent situation, the ruined-gift risk, and the care-is-the-gift lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make her a card' is the setup; the script adds the four-phase mission, the goat catastrophe, and the showing-your-love resolution. retagged: 'sad, kind' to 'sad, lonely' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed). vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
rows.per_story_synopsis: The grandbots' visit is canceled: Nana has the glitches and needs the day to recharge, and Doug is left holding confetti and a very sad antenna. Emma knows the cure, a handmade pick-me-up, so a newspaper becomes card stock, a memory becomes a daisy, and a starry sky gets painted blue. Then a goat eats the whole project. But the card that survives the goat is the story inside it, and Nana, low as she feels, gets picked all the way up by what the effort says, with everyone else feeling lighter too.
